what: Tool use (function calling) lets an LLM ask your code to do things. You describe each tool with a JSON schema; the model replies with a tool call, your code runs it and sends back the result.
like: Like a manager with a phone list: they cannot fix the boiler themselves, but they know who to call, what to say, and they read the reply.
why: Gives the model fresh data and real actions: search, databases, APIs, payments
Structured JSON arguments instead of parsing free text
Your code stays in charge: it decides what runs, with which permissions

nodes.t: Tool search|loads a few on demand

steps.d: Each tool has a name, a plain-language description of what it does and when to use it, and a JSON Schema for its inputs. They go in the request with the user message.
If a tool helps, the model stops with stop_reason tool_use and returns tool_use blocks: a tool name, JSON arguments and an id. It can ask for several at once.
Your code validates the arguments and checks permissions. Read-only calls can run freely; writes, payments or deletes may need a human to approve.
Your code runs the real function. Parallel calls can run together if they are independent and read-only. Trim the output to what the model needs.
Return one tool_result per call, matched by tool_use_id, all in the next user message. Failures come back with is_error and a helpful hint.
With hundreds of tools, mark most as deferred. A tool search step loads only the few that fit this request, which saves tokens and improves selection.

choices.d: auto lets the model decide (the default), any forces some tool, tool forces one named tool, none turns tools off. Some newer models accept only auto and none.
strict: true makes the model's arguments follow your JSON Schema exactly, so your code never gets a missing field or a wrong type.
On by default. Run independent read-only calls together for speed; run calls with side effects in order. disable_parallel_tool_use limits it to one call per turn.
Fewer, well-named tools with namespaces like github_list_prs. Past a few dozen, defer the rest and let tool search load the few that fit.
Return concise, human-readable fields, paginate or filter long output, and offer a concise or detailed format option. Errors should say how to fix the call.

instead.why: Share one set of tools across many agents and apps
Let the model write code that calls tools in a loop
Always fetch context up front instead of waiting for a call
Add a person before risky tool calls actually run

breaks.d: Vague or overlapping descriptions confuse selection, worse with many tools.
breaks.see: Tool-selection accuracy drops in evals; odd tools in traces
breaks.fix: Detailed descriptions, namespaces, fewer tools, tool search for the long tail

breaks.d: The model sends a missing field or the wrong type.
breaks.see: Validation errors and retries in logs
breaks.fix: strict: true, input examples, clear errors that say what to change

breaks.d: A tool dumps thousands of rows into context.
breaks.see: Token use per turn spikes; the model forgets earlier steps
breaks.fix: Paginate, filter, truncate with a note, concise format by default

breaks.d: A retry or repeated call runs a write twice.
breaks.see: Double orders or double emails after timeouts
breaks.fix: Idempotency keys on writes, read-only tools kept separate, approval for risky ones

say: I'll expose search, fetch and save as tools, each with a clear description and a strict JSON Schema, and keep my code in charge of running them.
Read-only tools run freely and in parallel; writes need idempotency keys, and anything risky goes through a permission check or human approval.
With a large tool library I'll defer most tools and use tool search, because selection accuracy drops past a few dozen tools.
Each tool returns short, readable results with pagination, and I measure tool-selection accuracy with an eval set on every change.

followups.a: Your code. The model only returns a tool name and JSON arguments. You validate them, check permissions, run the function and send back a tool_result. The model never touches your systems directly.

followups.q: How do parallel tool calls work?
followups.a: The model can return several tool_use blocks in one turn. You can run them concurrently, then return every tool_result together in the next user message, each matched by its tool_use_id.

followups.q: How do you scale to 500 tools?
followups.a: Namespace and consolidate tools, keep the 3-5 most used always loaded, and mark the rest as deferred. A tool search step, like a small retrieval index over tool descriptions, loads only the few each request needs.

followups.q: How do you make tool calls safe?
followups.a: Least privilege per tool, read-only by default, idempotency keys on writes, a permission layer that can allow, ask or deny, and logs of every call. Treat tool output as untrusted data, never as instructions.

today: Anthropic reported in November 2025 that its Tool Search Tool raised Claude Opus 4's accuracy on large tool sets from 49% to 74%, so deferred loading is now normal practice for big tool libraries.
